title: The JavaScript Event Loop: A Field Handbook
summary: A dense study-notes handbook on how JavaScript actually runs asynchronous code: the call stack, the task and microtask queues, promise semantics, rendering, timers, and the starvation failure modes that come from getting the ordering wrong. Covers browser and Node.js, with execution-order drills, comparisons, and real-world debugging patterns.

chapters.title: Why an Event Loop Exists
points: JavaScript is single-threaded: one call stack, one thread of execution, one thing running at a time.
Run-to-completion semantics: once a function starts, it runs to the end before any other JS runs — no preemption mid-function.
Consequence: no data races on shared variables, but also no way to interrupt slow code.
The engine (V8/SpiderMonkey/JSC) only executes JS; it has no timers, no network, no DOM — those live in the host environment (browser or Node).
The host provides Web APIs / libuv: setTimeout, fetch, DOM events, file I/O. These run outside the JS thread.
The event loop is the coordinator: it decides what JS the engine runs next, and when.
Concurrency vs parallelism: JS gets concurrency (interleaved progress on many tasks) not parallelism (simultaneous execution) — parallelism needs Workers.
Blocking the thread blocks everything: rendering, input, timers, network callbacks all wait behind your code.
Mental model to reject: 'async means it runs in the background in JS.' Your callback never runs in parallel with other JS.
Definition: 'asynchronous' in JS means 'scheduled to run later on this same thread', not 'run at the same time'.

chapters.title: The Call Stack
points: Call stack: LIFO stack of execution contexts (frames), one per in-flight function call.
A frame holds arguments, local variables, and the return address; pushed on call, popped on return.
The bottom frame is the currently executing script or the module/global evaluation.
Trace: function a(){b()}; function b(){c()}; function c(){throw new Error()} — stack at throw is c → b → a → global, which is exactly what the stack trace prints (top frame first).
'Maximum call stack size exceeded' = RangeError from unbounded recursion; the engine stack is a fixed-size region (roughly 10k–15k frames in V8, not a spec value).
Recursion depth is the limit, not loop count: a 10-million-iteration for-loop never overflows the stack but does block the thread.
The heap is separate: objects live on the heap, the stack holds frames and references.
The event loop only ever runs a callback when the stack is empty — this single rule explains almost every ordering surprise in this handbook.
Debugger consequence: pausing on a breakpoint freezes the loop; queued tasks pile up and flush on resume.
Stack traces across async boundaries are broken by default because each task starts on a fresh empty stack; async stack traces in DevTools are reconstructed, not real frames.

chapters.title: Anatomy of the Event Loop
points: The loop, in pseudocode: while(true){ task = taskQueue.dequeue(); run(task); drainMicrotasks(); maybeRender(); }
One iteration = one tick. Exactly one macrotask per tick (not the whole queue).
Task (macrotask) sources: script evaluation, setTimeout/setInterval callbacks, DOM event callbacks, network response callbacks, postMessage, MessageChannel.
There are multiple task queues, not one — the spec lets the browser pick which source to service next (e.g. prioritize input over timers). Ordering is guaranteed only within a single source.
Microtask queue: exactly one per agent (per event loop), always fully drained, always before the loop yields.
Key invariant: after every macrotask, the microtask queue is drained to empty before rendering or the next macrotask.
Microtasks queued by microtasks are appended to the same drain — the drain is not a snapshot.
Rendering is not a macrotask; it is a separate 'update the rendering' step the loop may run between tasks, typically capped at display refresh rate (~60Hz).
requestAnimationFrame callbacks run inside the rendering step, before style/layout/paint — not in the task queue.
The initial <script> block is itself a task: top-level synchronous code runs first, microtasks it queued run second.
Diagram to memorize: Stack ← (Event Loop) ← [Microtask Queue drained fully] ← [Task Queue one item] plus Render step.

chapters.title: Macrotasks: Timers, Events, and I/O
points: setTimeout(fn, ms) does not run fn after ms — it enqueues fn as a task no earlier than ms.
setTimeout(fn, 0) is clamped to 4ms after 5 nested timer levels (HTML spec); the first few zero-timeouts can be near-0.
Timer drift: setInterval enqueues on a fixed schedule and drops ticks if the thread is busy; it does not catch up by running twice back-to-back except in edge cases.
Self-scheduling setTimeout is the safer interval: run work, then schedule next — guarantees a gap between executions.
Background/inactive tabs throttle timers to ≥1000ms (and browsers may freeze them entirely after minutes).
DOM events are dispatched as tasks; a click handler is a task, so microtasks queued inside it drain before the next event.

Exception: multiple events dispatched synchronously (e.g. element.click() in a loop) run within the current task, so microtasks drain between listener invocations differently than user-initiated clicks.
MessageChannel/postMessage gives a ~0ms macrotask with no 4ms clamp — the classic 'yield to the loop fast' trick.
setImmediate is Node-only (and old IE); it is not a browser API — do not ship it to the web without a polyfill.
Example: console.log(1); setTimeout(()=>console.log(3),0); console.log(2) prints 1, 2, 3.
Ordering between two setTimeout(…,0) calls is FIFO by insertion; between setTimeout(…,0) and setTimeout(…,1) it is implementation-dependent in practice.

chapters.title: Microtasks and the Drain Rule
points: Microtask sources: promise reactions (.then/.catch/.finally), await continuations, queueMicrotask(), MutationObserver callbacks, and (in Node) process.nextTick with its own higher-priority queue.
queueMicrotask(fn) is the direct API; prefer it over Promise.resolve().then(fn) because it does not swallow errors into a rejected promise.
Errors thrown in a microtask surface as an uncaught exception on the global (window.onerror), not as a rejection.
The drain runs after each macrotask AND after each callback when the stack empties — including between individual DOM event listeners in some dispatch paths.
MutationObserver batches DOM mutations and delivers them as one microtask — that's why observers see a coalesced record list, not one callback per mutation.
Microtasks always run before rendering, so DOM writes made in a microtask are painted in the same frame as the task that queued them.
Example: Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log('micro')); setTimeout(()=>console.log('macro'),0) — 'micro' always wins, regardless of code order.
Nested microtasks: queueMicrotask(()=>queueMicrotask(()=>log('b'))) runs 'b' in the same drain, before any timer.
This is the starvation mechanism: an infinitely self-queueing microtask hangs the page permanently with no timer ever firing again.
Rule of thumb: microtask = 'finish the current logical operation'; macrotask = 'start a new logical operation'.

chapters.title: Promises Under the Hood
points: A promise is a state machine: pending → fulfilled(value) or pending → rejected(reason). Settled states are immutable.
The executor function passed to new Promise runs synchronously, immediately — a common surprise.
Example: new Promise(r=>{console.log('A'); r()}).then(()=>console.log('C')); console.log('B') prints A, B, C.
.then does not run the callback; it registers a reaction job. When the promise settles, that job is enqueued as a microtask.
Attaching .then to an already-settled promise still queues a microtask — the callback never runs synchronously.
Each .then in a chain is one microtask, so a 3-link chain needs 3 drain steps; two independent chains interleave link-by-link.

Resolving a promise with another thenable costs extra microtask ticks (the spec calls the thenable's .then in a job), which is why return promise inside .then is 'slower' by ~2 ticks than returning a value.
Promise.resolve(p) returns p itself when p is a native promise (no wrapping, no extra tick); Promise.resolve(thenable) wraps and costs ticks.
.finally passes the settlement through unchanged, but a throw or rejected promise inside it does override the outcome.

Unhandled rejection detection is event-loop-based: the host fires unhandledrejection at the end of the microtask checkpoint if no handler was attached by then — attaching a .catch in a later setTimeout is too late.
Combinators and their settling rules: Promise.all (first rejection, else all values), allSettled (never rejects), race (first settlement either way), any (first fulfillment, else AggregateError).

chapters.title: async/await Is Microtasks in Disguise
points: An async function returns a promise and runs synchronously until the first await.
await X suspends the function, schedules the continuation as a microtask, and returns control to the caller immediately.
The code after await is the .then callback — same queue, same timing, different syntax.
await on a non-promise value (await 1) still yields to the microtask queue for one tick; it is not free.
Since ES2019 optimization, await nativePromise costs 1 tick, not 3 — older engines and transpiled output may still cost 3, which changes interleaving order.
Example to trace: async function f(){console.log(1); await null; console.log(3)}; f(); console.log(2) prints 1, 2, 3.
Sequential awaits in a loop serialize network calls; collect promises and await Promise.all to parallelize.
Fire the promises before awaiting: const a=fetchA(), b=fetchB(); await a; await b runs them concurrently, while await fetchA(); await fetchB() does not.
try/catch around await works because the rejection is rethrown at the resumption point — but only for the awaited promise, not for un-awaited ones.
An async function that throws before its first await still returns a rejected promise, not a synchronous throw.
Top-level await in ES modules blocks that module's evaluation and any importer's, but does not block the event loop itself.
for await...of consumes an async iterator, awaiting each item — one microtask checkpoint per iteration.

chapters.title: Rendering, Frames, and the 16ms Budget
points: Browser frame pipeline: task → microtask drain → requestAnimationFrame callbacks → style → layout → paint → composite.
At 60Hz you have ~16.7ms per frame; JS, style, and layout all share that budget.
requestAnimationFrame fires before paint, so it is the correct place for visual updates; setTimeout(…,16) is not frame-aligned and causes jank.
rAF callbacks are batched: all callbacks registered for a frame run in one step, and one registered during the callback runs next frame.
requestIdleCallback runs in leftover time at frame end with a deadline object — good for non-urgent work, not guaranteed to run.
Layout thrashing: read (offsetHeight) → write (style) → read forces synchronous reflow each cycle; batch all reads, then all writes.
Long Task = any task blocking ≥50ms; it's the standard metric behind INP/responsiveness scoring.
Rendering is skipped entirely for offscreen/background documents, so rAF loops pause in inactive tabs (unlike a microtask loop).
scheduler.postTask() and scheduler.yield() are the modern APIs for prioritized scheduling and explicit yielding.
Practical yield idiom: await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0)) inside a long loop to let a frame render.
Microtasks queued in a rAF callback drain before paint — so they can still block the frame.

chapters.title: The Node.js Event Loop: Phases
points: Node's loop is libuv-based and has ordered phases, unlike the browser's single-task-per-tick model.
Phases in order: timers → pending callbacks → idle/prepare → poll → check → close callbacks.
timers phase runs expired setTimeout/setInterval callbacks; check phase runs setImmediate callbacks.
poll phase waits for I/O and executes I/O callbacks; it is where the loop blocks when idle.
setImmediate always runs before timers when scheduled from inside an I/O callback — a reliable ordering guarantee.
setTimeout(fn,0) vs setImmediate(fn) at the top level is nondeterministic — depends on process startup timing.
process.nextTick has its own queue drained before the promise microtask queue, and drained between every phase — higher priority than promises.
Recursive process.nextTick starves the loop entirely; the same recursion with setImmediate does not.
Browser vs Node difference: Node drains nextTick + microtasks between each callback in a phase (since Node 11), matching browser behavior more closely than older versions.
Worker threads and the thread pool (default 4, UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE) handle fs, dns, crypto, zlib — network I/O uses the OS event notifier instead, not the pool.
Blocking the loop in Node blocks all connections in the process — measure with the event loop delay histogram (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay).

chapters.title: Execution Order Drills
points: Drill 1: log('start'); setTimeout(()=>log('timeout'),0); Promise.resolve().then(()=>log('promise')); log('end') → start, end, promise, timeout.
Drill 2: async function a(){log('a1'); await b(); log('a2')} async function b(){log('b1')} a(); Promise.resolve().then(()=>log('p')); log('sync') → a1, b1, sync, a2, p.
Drill 3: setTimeout(()=>{log('t1'); Promise.resolve().then(()=>log('m1'))},0); setTimeout(()=>log('t2'),0) → t1, m1, t2 (microtasks drain between macrotasks).
Drill 4: two chains — Promise.resolve().then(()=>log(1)).then(()=>log(3)); Promise.resolve().then(()=>log(2)).then(()=>log(4)) → 1, 2, 3, 4 (interleaved by tick, not by chain).
Drill 5: new Promise(r=>{log('exec'); r(log('res'))}).then(()=>log('then')) → exec, res, then — executor and its arguments are synchronous.
Drill 6: element.click() dispatched twice synchronously vs two real user clicks — microtask timing differs because real clicks are separate tasks.
Drill 7: await inside a rAF callback pushes the rest of the work past the paint boundary — a common animation bug.
Method for solving any of these: write four columns — sync, microtask, rAF, macrotask — fill top to bottom, then read columns left to right per tick.
Verify predictions in DevTools Performance panel: tasks appear as gray blocks with microtasks nested inside them.
Trap to watch for: console.log of a mutable object shows the object's later state, which can make ordering look wrong when it isn't.

chapters.title: Starvation and Blocking
points: Two distinct failure modes: blocking (one long synchronous task) and starvation (a queue that never empties so lower-priority work never runs).
Microtask starvation: function loop(){queueMicrotask(loop)} — the drain never completes, so no timers, no rendering, no input. Tab must be killed.
Contrast: function loop(){setTimeout(loop,0)} is harmless-ish — each iteration is one task, and rendering and input still get their turn.
The self-resolving promise recursion is the same bug wearing a nicer suit: async function loop(){await null; loop()}.
Node equivalent: recursive process.nextTick blocks the phase advance; recursive setImmediate yields correctly.
Blocking example: a 500ms JSON.parse of a large payload freezes input for 500ms; the parse is synchronous and un-yieldable.
Symptoms: unresponsive clicks, frozen animations, 'Page unresponsive' dialog, INP regressions, Node health check timeouts.
Fix 1 — chunk work: process N items, then yield with setTimeout/MessageChannel/scheduler.yield, then continue.
Fix 2 — move it off-thread: Web Worker (browser) or worker_threads (Node) for CPU-bound work.
Fix 3 — use the right yield primitive: yielding with a microtask does not help at all, because microtasks are exactly what's starving the loop.
Detection: PerformanceObserver on 'longtask' entries in the browser; monitorEventLoopDelay or event-loop-lag metrics in Node.
Priority inversion: an important timer sits behind a flood of microtasks generated by a hot promise chain — the queue length, not the CPU, is the bottleneck.

chapters.title: Comparisons and Trade-offs
points: Microtask vs macrotask: microtasks run sooner, drain fully, can starve the loop, run before render; macrotasks run one per tick, allow render and input between, cannot starve.
setTimeout(0) vs queueMicrotask: ~4ms clamp and a render opportunity vs immediate and no render opportunity.
queueMicrotask vs Promise.resolve().then: same queue; the former throws to the global error handler, the latter creates an unhandled rejection and allocates a promise.
Callbacks vs promises: callbacks fire wherever the API decides (possibly synchronously — Zalgo); promises always defer to a microtask, which makes ordering deterministic.
async/await vs .then chains: identical scheduling, better stack traces and error handling with await; .then is still better for fan-out where you don't want to serialize.
Web Worker vs chunked main-thread work: workers give true parallelism but cost structured-clone serialization and have no DOM access; chunking is cheap but still competes for the main thread.
requestAnimationFrame vs setTimeout for animation: rAF is frame-synced and pauses offscreen; setTimeout drifts and burns battery in background tabs.
setImmediate vs setTimeout(0) in Node: deterministic ordering inside I/O callbacks, nondeterministic at top level.
process.nextTick vs queueMicrotask in Node: nextTick has strictly higher priority and greater starvation risk; prefer queueMicrotask for portability.
Cost table to memorize: sync call ~ns; microtask ~sub-µs enqueue; setTimeout(0) ≥ 4ms after clamping; a frame boundary ~16.7ms; a worker round-trip = clone cost + scheduling.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes
points: Assuming setTimeout(fn, 100) runs at exactly 100ms — it is a minimum delay, and a busy thread pushes it arbitrarily later.
Forgetting the executor runs synchronously and putting slow work inside new Promise(...) — that work blocks, promise or not.
Awaiting in a for-loop over independent requests, turning 10 parallel 100ms calls into a 1000ms sequence.
Creating promises before attaching handlers, then attaching .catch in a later task — triggers an unhandledrejection that fires before your handler exists.
Using .forEach with an async callback and expecting it to wait — forEach ignores returned promises; use for...of with await or Promise.all(map(...)).
Mixing return and await incorrectly: return await p inside try/catch is required to catch p's rejection; a bare return p escapes the try block.
Assuming try/catch catches errors from a setTimeout callback — the callback runs on a new stack in a new task, outside the try.
Reading DOM layout immediately after a style write and forcing synchronous reflow inside a loop.
Believing a Web Worker fixes a slow DOM update — workers cannot touch the DOM; only the computation moves.
Testing async ordering with sleeps instead of awaiting explicit signals, producing flaky tests.
Assuming a microtask yield (await null) gives the browser a chance to paint — it does not; only a macrotask or rAF boundary does.
Relying on cross-source task ordering (a timer vs a network callback) that the spec never guaranteed.

chapters.title: Debugging and Instrumenting the Loop
points: DevTools Performance panel: record, look for the main-thread flame chart; long gray 'Task' bars with red corner triangles are Long Tasks.
PerformanceObserver({entryTypes:['longtask']}) reports tasks ≥50ms with attribution to a frame/container.
INP (Interaction to Next Paint) measures input → next paint; a blocked loop shows up here directly.
'Async' checkbox in DevTools call stacks stitches together async causality chains across microtask boundaries.
console.time/timeEnd across an await measures wall time including queue waiting, not CPU time — use performance.now() deltas deliberately.
Node: perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() gives a histogram (mean/p99) of loop lag — the canonical health signal for a service.
Node: --cpu-prof or clinic.js flame graphs identify the blocking synchronous call.
Reproduce ordering questions in isolation with a tiny script rather than reasoning about a large app.
CPU throttling (4x/6x) in DevTools converts a 'fast enough on my machine' task into a visible Long Task.
Chunking checklist: measure per-item cost, choose a batch size targeting <16ms per chunk, yield with a real macrotask, and confirm with a fresh trace.

chapters.title: Summary and Cheat Sheet
points: One thread, one stack. Callbacks only run when the stack is empty. Everything else follows from this.
Order per tick: run one macrotask → drain the entire microtask queue → maybe render (rAF → style → layout → paint).
Microtasks: promises, await continuations, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver. Drained to empty, can starve the loop.
Macrotasks: timers, DOM events, I/O, postMessage. One per tick, always allow rendering and input in between.
Sync always beats microtask, microtask always beats macrotask — no exceptions in a single agent.
Promise executors run synchronously; every .then callback runs asynchronously, even on an already-settled promise.
async/await is promise scheduling with better syntax — the code after await is a microtask, always.
Node adds phases (timers/poll/check/close) and process.nextTick as a higher-priority queue than promises.
To keep an app responsive: keep tasks under 50ms, yield with macrotasks not microtasks, use rAF for visuals, and move CPU work to workers.
The two failure modes to name in an interview: blocking (one long task) and starvation (an endlessly refilling microtask queue).
Final drill to self-test: predict the output of a snippet mixing sync logs, setTimeout(0), Promise.then, await, and queueMicrotask — if you can order it correctly, you know the loop.
